extra.message: Hardcoded Flask Secret Key enabling session forgery — An attacker with access to the source code can forge Flask session cookies to impersonate any user (including admins), gaining full unauthorized access to all accounts and data. [verified: app.py:11 hardcodes app.secret_key = 'super secret key' with no environment-variable override or config fallback; Flask signs all session cookies with this key, so anyone who reads the public source can forge valid sessions for any user including admins.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via render_template_string with user-controlled request.path — Remote code execution, full server compromise, exposure of all secrets and database contents [verified: Same SSTI as [0] — user-controlled request.path flows unsanitized into render_template_string via f-string in the 404 handler; no before_request or middleware validates the URL path.]

SQL Injection in note search via f-string SQL LIKE clause — Unauthorized data access to all notes and database contents, data exfiltration [verified: Same as finding [0] — search_param from request.args.get('search','') interpolated unescaped into text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'") at line 30-33, with no parameterization or sanitization between attacker input and raw SQL sink.]

Mass Assignment / Privilege Escalation via unfiltered is_admin field in account update — Any authenticated user can grant themselves admin privileges, gaining access to registration code management and all users' data [verified: Same as finding [3] — the filtered_values comprehension at lines 68-81 excludes only None values and 'password', letting is_admin=true from the POST body directly update current_user.__dict__, granting any authenticated user admin privileges.]

Mass Assignment / Privilege Escalation — any user can set is_admin=True via account update form — Any authenticated user can escalate to administrator by sending is_admin=True in the account update POST, gaining access to registration code management, all user notes, and full administrative control. [verified: AccountForm includes is_admin BooleanField; the filtered_values dict comprehension at line 76-79 only excludes None values and the 'password' key, allowing is_admin to pass through into current_user.__dict__.update() — any authenticated attacker can POST is_admin=true and escalate to admin regardless of template hiding.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads on user-controlled cookie — Remote code execution on the server, full application compromise [verified: Same as findings [1] and [5] — user-controlled preferences cookie is fed to pickle.loads(b64decode(preferences)) at line 96 in before_request with no integrity verification, enabling arbitrary code execution on every request.]

Insecure Deserialization — pickle.loads on user-controlled preferences cookie — Remote code execution on the server via a crafted cookie, leading to full server compromise. [verified: User-controlled preferences cookie value is base64-decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads() at line 118 without any HMAC, signature verification, or restricted unpickler — attacker-crafted pickle payload achieves arbitrary code execution on any request.]

SQL Injection in signup registration code validation via raw f-string SQL — Bypass registration code protection to create accounts without a valid invite code, plus arbitrary database access. [verified: validate_token() at line 15-17 interpolates form.registration_code.data into text(f"...WHERE code = '{code}'") with zero parameterization; only Length(min=5) guards the field, which passes SQL metacharacters unchanged.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via user-supplied image URL in urlopen — Access to internal network resources, cloud metadata service exploitation, internal service enumeration [verified: Same SSRF sink as finding [0]: form.url.data → urlopen(url) at profile_image.py:7-8. No scheme restrictions exist — attacker can supply http://localhost/, http://169.254.169.254/, or internal Docker addresses. ImageForm URLField only validates URL format, not destination.]

IDOR — Cross-user private note access via /accounts/<user_id>/notes — Unauthorized access to any user's private notes, including admin users' sensitive notes [verified: Same as findings [2], [7], and [10] — /accounts/<int:user_id>/notes at line 39 filters notes solely by path-supplied user_id with no ownership or admin authorization check, exposing all users' private notes.]

Missing CSRF Protection on all state-changing POST routes — Attackers can perform unauthorized actions on behalf of authenticated users — change account details, escalate to admin (combined with mass assignment), create/delete notes, change profile images, and manage registration codes. [verified: All state-changing POST routes use plain wtforms.Form (not Flask-WTF FlaskForm) with no CSRF tokens in templates; Flask-WTF is listed in requirements.txt but never imported or configured, and no CSRF middleware exists — cross-site request forgery is unmitigated on login, signup, account, image, darkmode, notes, and registration-codes endpoints.]

Missing rate limiting on login and signup endpoints — Brute-force attacks on user passwords and registration codes are trivially possible [verified: Identical evidence to findings 0 and 2: no rate-limiting mechanism exists anywhere in the codebase for login or signup endpoints, allowing unlimited brute-force password and registration-code guessing.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing POST routes — Cross-site request forgery enabling forced note creation/deletion, account modification, privilege escalation, and other state changes [verified: All 5 form classes extend wtforms.Form (not Flask-WTF's FlaskForm); Flask-WTF is installed but never imported; codebase grep for csrf_token|CSRFProtect|WTF_CSRF returns zero matches; every state-changing POST route (/login, /signup, /notes, /account, /account/image, /notes/<id>/delete, /darkmode, /registration-codes) lacks CSRF tokens.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing POST routes — Cross-site request forgery — attackers can force authenticated users to create/delete notes, change account settings, or toggle dark mode without their knowledge [verified: All forms extend wtforms.Form (not flask_wtf.FlaskForm), templates contain no hidden CSRF token fields, and no CSRF middleware or SameSite cookie attributes exist. Every state-changing POST route (/notes, /notes/<id>/delete, /account, /account/image, /darkmode, /registration-codes, /login, /signup) is unprotected.]

IDOR — Unauthorized note deletion without ownership check — Any authenticated user can delete any other user's notes, causing data loss [verified: Same endpoint — delete_note() retrieves the note by ID and deletes it unconditionally. No `note.user_id == current_user.id` or `current_user.is_admin` check exists anywhere on the server path, making this a genuine IDOR.]

Missing Authorization — any authenticated user can delete any note — Arbitrary deletion of any user's notes, including private notes and admin notes, causing data loss and denial of service. [verified: delete_note() at routes/notes.py:39-52 checks only `note is None`; no server-side ownership check (`note.user_id == current_user.id` or `current_user.is_admin`). The template hides the delete button client-side but any authenticated user can POST to /notes/<any_id>/delete.]

Missing CSRF protection on POST /notes/<id>/delete — An attacker can force a victim's browser to delete their notes via a cross-site request, causing data loss. [verified: No CSRF protection exists anywhere in the app — wtforms.Form (not FlaskForm) is used, no flask_wtf, no WTF_CSRF config, no custom CSRF tokens, and no SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE is configured. The delete endpoint also lacks ownership checks, so any authenticated user's session can be exploited via CSRF to delete any note, causing data loss.]

User and registration-code enumeration via distinct signup error messages — Enumeration of valid registration codes and registered email addresses; targeted credential attacks [verified: Distinct flash messages 'Invalid registration code' (line 47) vs 'User already exists' (line 60) enable enumeration of both valid invite codes and registered emails; code enumeration is more severe because invite codes are authentication secrets with no brute-force protection.]

Stored XSS via uncontrolled MIME type in profile image data URI — Attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browsers of all users who view the attacker's profile image on any page (home page notes, account page, navbar), enabling session theft, credential harvesting, and arbitrary actions on behalf of victim users. [verified: get_base64_image_blob() at profile_image.py:13 uses guess_type(url)[0] on attacker-supplied URL to set MIME type with zero validation. An attacker URL ending in .html yields text/html; the resulting data:text/html;base64,... URI is stored in DB and rendered in <object> tags (base.html:61, home.html:36, account.html:43). <object> tags execute JavaScript from HTML data URIs. No CSP headers exist any]

Sensitive data exposure via SQLAlchemy echo=True logging all SQL queries — Exposure of user emails, bcrypt password hashes, and private note content in application logs [verified: Same echo=True config as finding 0; every parameterized SQL query (including SELECT of password hashes, INSERT of emails/notes/codes) is logged to stdout and captured by Docker container logs with no suppression.]

Missing CSRF protection on POST /account/image — An attacker can trigger SSRF through a victim's session by forcing their browser to submit a profile image URL via a cross-site request. [verified: No CSRF protection exists anywhere — no Flask-WTF CSRF, no CSRF middleware, forms extend bare wtforms.Form; POST /account/image is state-changing (profile image update) and reachable with an authenticated session, enabling CSRF→SSRF chain.]

Missing authentication on POST /account update endpoint — Unauthenticated users can reach the account update handler. Currently results in a server error, but a code change could enable unauthenticated account modification. [verified: POST /account at line 68 lacks @login_required while GET /account at line 19 has it; the function accesses current_user.__dict__ on an unauthenticated request, and no compensating auth control exists on this state-changing endpoint.]

Missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags on cookies — Session and preference cookies can be stolen via MITM on non-HTTPS connections or via XSS (preferences cookie readable by JS), enabling session hijacking [verified: Both the preferences cookie (set via response.set_cookie() at line 88 with no flags) and the Flask session cookie (no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True configured anywhere) can be transmitted over cleartext HTTP — nginx listens on port 80 with no HTTPS/TLS termination, so session hijacking via MITM is viable on the deployed path.]

Insecure cookie flags — preferences cookie missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite — Cookie accessible to JavaScript (XSS exfiltration), transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, sent in cross-origin requests; widens deserialization attack surface [verified: Same as finding [8] — the preferences cookie set via response.set_cookie() at line 105 lacks Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes, exposing the pickle-serialized cookie to JavaScript access, cleartext transmission, and cross-site requests.]

Missing Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite flags on preferences cookie — Cookie accessible via XSS (HttpOnly missing), transmitted in cleartext (Secure missing), sent on cross-site requests (SameSite missing) [verified: response.set_cookie('preferences',...) at line 108 in toggle_darkmode sets no secure, httponly, or samesite flags — the cookie is transmitted over cleartext HTTP, accessible to JavaScript, and sent on cross-site requests, widening the attack surface for the pickle deserialization vulnerability.]

Missing CSRF protection on POST /registration-codes — An attacker can force an admin's browser to generate new registration codes via a cross-site request, enabling unauthorized access to the invitation system. [verified: No CSRF protection exists anywhere in the app: forms use plain wtforms.Form (not FlaskForm), templates lack csrf_token fields, no CSRF middleware or SameSite cookie attribute is configured, and Flask-WTF is installed but never imported or initialized. The POST /registration-codes endpoint at line 26 is reachable, protected only by @login_required and is_admin check—both satisfied by the victim's s]

Missing rate limiting on signup endpoint enabling brute-force attacks — An attacker can brute-force registration codes and create accounts in bulk, enabling spam, resource exhaustion, and abuse of the invitation system. [verified: No rate limiting exists anywhere — no Flask-Limiter in requirements.txt, no limit_req in nginx.conf, no throttle decorators on the signup route handler, and no uwsgi rate controls; the endpoint is publicly reachable with no auth barrier.]

Missing CSRF protection on POST /signup — An attacker can force a victim's browser to create an account with attacker-chosen credentials via a cross-site request. [verified: CSRF protection is completely absent — the app uses plain WTForms (not FlaskForm), no CSRFProtect middleware is initialized in app.py, signup.html has no csrf_token field, and no CSRF check is performed in the route handler; all POST forms across the app share this missing control.]

User enumeration via distinct signup error messages — Attackers can compile a list of valid email addresses for targeted phishing or credential-stuffing attacks [verified: Same distinct-error enumeration as findings [1] and [3] at line 60; the 'User already exists' flash allows an attacker to confirm valid email addresses once past the broken code gate, with no rate limiting or uniform error response.]

Denial of Service via unbounded HTTP response read in profile image download — An attacker can exhaust server memory and crash the application process, causing denial of service for all users. Repeated attacks can keep the service unavailable. [verified: response.read() at profile_image.py:8 reads the entire HTTP response into memory with no Content-Length check, no max-size cap, and urlopen defaults to timeout=None. An attacker-supplied URL pointing to a multi-gigabyte file or slow-streaming endpoint will exhaust server RAM and crash the Flask process.]

Unbounded memory consumption via profile image URL download — Denial of service — server memory exhaustion leading to process crash or system-wide OOM kill, denying service to all users. [verified: Same unbounded resource consumption as finding [1]: response.read() at profile_image.py:8 with no size/timeout guard. Attacker provides URL to /dev/urandom, a ZIP bomb, or a slow-loris endpoint; entire body is buffered in memory then base64-encoded, amplifying memory pressure until OOM.]

Missing CSRF protection on POST /darkmode — An attacker can toggle a victim's dark mode preference via a cross-site request, a minor nuisance but indicates systematic CSRF absence. [verified: Same global absence of CSRF protection; POST /darkmode modifies the preferences cookie and is reachable without CSRF token validation, though impact is limited to toggling dark mode.]
